$comment: Everyday stories, noun Concept, part 4 of 4 (presentationMetadata, referenceDefinition, schemaObject, seed, sequence). Same style rules as stories-pilot.json. Owner reviews each part.

stories.presentationMetadata.column: In a form with two columns, the phone box belongs on the right, next to the e-mail. Column says which grid column a box sits in, counting from one. The form reads like a paper one, and not like a long ladder.
stories.presentationMetadata.columnSpan: A short postal code box needs one column, but the address needs the full width. Column span says how many grid columns a box takes. Wide things get room, small things do not waste it.
stories.presentationMetadata.currency: A price of 1500 means little until the screen says 'R$ 1.500,00'. Currency gives the money code, such as BRL, and the number is shown as money with the right symbol and separators.
stories.presentationMetadata.customWidgetRef: Sometimes no ready-made control fits, such as a signature pad or a seat map. With a custom widget, this keyword names the component, supplied with the app, that draws that box. Everything else on the form stays standard.
stories.presentationMetadata.defaultGroup: A list of tasks can also be a board with columns, such as To do, Doing and Done. Default group names the choice box whose values become the columns. If you do not say, the lifecycle's status box is used.
stories.presentationMetadata.defaultSort: People open the list of invoices and expect the newest first. Default sort names the box the list is ordered by when the person has not chosen anything. The first view is already useful.
stories.presentationMetadata.deprecated: The 'fax' box is no longer used, but old records still have numbers in it. Deprecated keeps it for old data and hides it from new entries. Nothing is lost and no one is tempted to fill it in again.
stories.presentationMetadata.description: A box labelled 'Ref' leaves people guessing. Description is one sentence of help next to the control, such as 'The number printed on the supplier's invoice'. It answers the doubt right where it appears.
stories.presentationMetadata.displayMode: Records can be shown as a plain table, as cards or as a board. Display mode is the way the concept's records are shown by default. People start with the view that suits the data.
stories.presentationMetadata.enabledWhen: A 'discount reason' box makes sense only when a discount was given. Enabled when is a condition on the record: the box can be edited only while it is true. Otherwise it is greyed out, and nobody fills it in by mistake.
stories.presentationMetadata.formColumns: A form with fifteen boxes in one long column forces endless scrolling. Form columns sets how many columns the create and edit form has, one by default. Two or three make it fit on a desktop screen.
stories.presentationMetadata.formPresentation: Creating a record can replace the list with the form, with a 'Back to list' button, or open a small pop-up over the list. Form presentation picks which one. Quick notes like a pop-up, long forms like the full page.
stories.presentationMetadata.group: In a customer form, the phone and the e-mail belong together under 'Contact'. Group names the cluster a box belongs to. Boxes with the same group are drawn side by side under one heading.
stories.presentationMetadata.imageField: A list of products is much easier to scan with a small picture of each one. Image field names the box of the target that holds a picture, and it appears as the thumbnail when someone chooses it. It is easier to pick the right item.
stories.presentationMetadata.label: Behind the scenes a box is called 'birthDt', but the screen should say 'Date of birth', or 'Data de nascimento' in Portuguese. Label is the name people read, a plain text or one per language. If you leave it out, a tidied-up version of the name is used.
stories.presentationMetadata.listColumn: A list of customers shows name and phone, not the 40 other boxes. List column says whether a box is a column of the list. Set it to false to keep the list light.
stories.presentationMetadata.listColumnOrder: On the list people want the name first, then the city, then the balance. List column order gives each column its position, lower first. The table reads in the order of importance.
stories.presentationMetadata.offlineWrite: A delivery driver loses signal in a tunnel but still has to record a delivery. Offline write lets the app queue the changes on the device and send them when the signal returns, marked as pending. If someone else changed the record meanwhile, the app asks the driver to redo it, and never overwrites.
stories.presentationMetadata.order: A form should ask for the name before the phone, and not in the order the boxes were written. Order gives each box its position in forms and details, lower first. People fill it in the natural sequence.
stories.presentationMetadata.placeholder: An empty box that shows 'e.g. Ana Souza' in light grey tells people what to type. Placeholder is that grey hint text inside an empty input. It disappears as soon as they start writing.
stories.presentationMetadata.readonlyWhen: Once an invoice is paid, its amount should no longer be editable. Readonly when is a condition: while it is true, the box can be read but not changed. It protects the record exactly when it matters.
stories.presentationMetadata.requiredWhen: A 'reason for refusal' is needed only when the request is refused. Required when is a condition on the record: while it is true, the box is marked and enforced as required. The rest of the time, it can stay empty.
stories.presentationMetadata.searchFields: When people type in the customer picker, they may type a name, a tax number or a phone. Search fields are the boxes the picker looks at for that text. They find the right person however they remember them.
stories.presentationMetadata.section: A long form is easier as titled blocks, such as 'Personal data' and 'Address'. Section names the block a box sits in. People can see where they are and skip what is not for them.
stories.presentationMetadata.selectionTools: A clerk ticks twelve rows in a list and wants to compare them, paste them into a spreadsheet or download them. Selection tools offer exactly those three actions on the ticked rows. They are on unless you turn them off for a concept.
stories.presentationMetadata.shortLabel: A column header called 'Estimated delivery date' fills a phone screen. Short label is a shorter name used where space is tight, such as table headers or mobile cards. The full name stays in the form.
stories.presentationMetadata.showInDefaultWebUi: An internal box such as 'sync marker' is no use to anyone on screen. Setting this to false hides it from the generated web screens entirely, while it stays available to the app's interface for other programs.
stories.presentationMetadata.summaryCard: On a record's little summary card, people want the name, the status and the owner, not everything. Summary card marks the boxes shown there. The essentials are visible at a glance.
stories.presentationMetadata.tab: A big record, like an employee, is easier when split into tabs: Personal, Contract, Documents. Tab names the tab a box sits on. People open only what they need.
stories.presentationMetadata.visibleWhen: A 'company name' box only matters if the customer is a company. Visible when is a condition on the record: the control appears only while it is true. A private person never sees the box.
stories.presentationMetadata.widget: A yes-or-no is best as a tick box, a story as a big text area, a choice as a dropdown. Widget names the control used to edit a box, and it must suit the box's kind. The validator checks it.
stories.presentationMetadata.width: A postal code needs a narrow box and an address a wide one. Width gives the preferred width of a control or column, as a size or a keyword. The form looks balanced instead of every box being the same.
stories.referenceDefinition.defaultFilter: When someone picks a customer for an invoice, blocked customers should not appear. Default filter is a condition that limits which target rows the picker offers. People cannot choose what they should not.
stories.referenceDefinition.displayField: An order should say 'Ana Souza', not 'customer 4711'. Display field names the box of the target used as the readable text of a reference. People see names, and the app keeps the numbers.
stories.referenceDefinition.displayTemplate: A product reads best as 'P-100 - Cotton towel', not as just a code or just a name. Display template combines several boxes of the target into one line, with a pattern like code, dash, name. People see everything they need in one glance.
stories.referenceDefinition.inlineCreate: When the customer you want does not exist yet, you may want to create it from the picker. Inline create allows or hides that option. 'Deny' makes sure only the proper customer screen creates customers.
stories.referenceDefinition.multiple: A task may have several assignees, not just one. Multiple makes the box hold a list of references instead of one. People can add as many as they need.
stories.referenceDefinition.onDelete: What happens to the orders when you delete their customer? On delete decides: restrict refuses the deletion, cascade removes the orders too, nullify just clears the link. You choose how much a deletion may break.
stories.referenceDefinition.pickerColumns: The window that opens to choose a product should show code, name and price, not twenty columns. Picker columns are the target's boxes shown there. People compare options quickly.
stories.referenceDefinition.previewCardTemplate: When someone has chosen a customer, a small card can show name, city and phone together. The preview card template is the pattern for that card. They confirm they picked the right one without opening it.
stories.referenceDefinition.previewFields: Hovering over a chosen customer can reveal a few more details. Preview fields are the boxes of the target shown in that pop-up. The person checks without leaving the form.
stories.referenceDefinition.searchFields: People find customers by typing a surname, a tax number or an e-mail. Search fields are the boxes of the target that the picker searches while they type. It finds the person whichever detail they remember.
stories.referenceDefinition.target: An order must say which kind of record it points at. Target is the name of that concept, such as 'Customer', or a pack-qualified one such as 'identity::User'. The app keeps the link valid.
stories.referenceDefinition.via: Normally a link points at the target's hidden id. Via points at another box instead, such as the product code, if that box is the id or a unique box marked as an anchor. People and files then use the code they know.
stories.schemaObject.default: A fixed starting value for a part of a structure, such as country 'BR' in an address. It is used when the person writes nothing. If they type something, theirs wins.
stories.schemaObject.defaultExpression: A starting value that comes from a short formula, such as today's date. Default expression gives the value of a part of a structure when none is written. It fills the gap by itself.
stories.schemaObject.derivedExpression: Inside a structure, a total is computed from its siblings: quantity times price. Derived expression gives the formula, so the value is always consistent and never typed by hand.
stories.schemaObject.description: A sentence saying what a part of a structure means, such as 'street and number, without the city'. Anyone filling it in, or an AI writing it, knows what belongs there.
stories.schemaObject.duplicationPolicy: In a list of attachments inside a structure, the same file should not appear twice. Duplication policy allows or refuses elements that share the same identity. One word keeps the list clean.
stories.schemaObject.enumValues: A part of a structure may only be 'home', 'work' or 'other'. Enum values lists the allowed choices. Anything else is refused.
stories.schemaObject.itemIdentityField: In a list of phone numbers inside a structure, two entries are 'the same' when they share the number. Item identity field names the property that identifies an element. It works together with the duplication policy.
stories.schemaObject.items: A list inside a structure needs a description of each element, such as 'an object with a street and a city'. Items gives that description, and it applies to every element.
stories.schemaObject.max: A number inside a structure may not go above a limit, such as a percentage of 100. Max is the largest value allowed. Above it, the value is refused.
stories.schemaObject.maxItems: A list inside a structure may hold at most, say, three phone numbers. Max items sets that limit. The fourth is refused.
stories.schemaObject.maxLength: A text inside a structure may not be longer than, say, 40 letters. Max length sets the limit. A longer text is refused and the person is told so.
stories.schemaObject.min: A number inside a structure may not go below a limit, such as zero. Min is the smallest value allowed. Below it, the value is refused.
stories.schemaObject.minItems: A list inside a structure needs at least one element, such as one contact. Min items sets that minimum. An empty list is refused.
stories.schemaObject.minLength: A text inside a structure may not be shorter than, say, three letters. Min length sets that minimum. A shorter text is refused.
stories.schemaObject.precision: A decimal number inside a structure may have at most so many digits in total. Precision sets it, up to 38. A typo like an extra zero does not become a million.
stories.schemaObject.properties: A structure, such as an address, is made of named parts: street, number, city. Properties lists those parts, each with its own description. The whole behaves like one box on the form.
stories.schemaObject.regex: A tax number has a fixed shape, such as three digits, a dash and two digits. Regex describes that shape. A text that does not fit it is refused.
stories.schemaObject.required: An address structure without a city is useless. Required lists the parts that must be present. If one is missing, the whole structure is refused.
stories.schemaObject.scale: A decimal number inside a structure may keep two digits after the point. Scale sets how many. The value is neither cut nor invented in reports.
stories.schemaObject.type: Each part of a structure has a kind: text, number, date, a list, another structure or a reference. Type says which. The rest of the description follows from it.
stories.schemaObject.uniqueItems: In a list inside a structure, all elements should differ, such as the days of the week a shop opens. Unique items refuses a list with two equal elements.
stories.seed.alias: When you create sample data, an order must point at a customer you just created. An alias is a short name given to a sample record, so later ones can refer to it. It must be unique among all the samples.
stories.seed.concept: Sample data must say which kind of record it creates, such as 'Customer'. Concept names it. A pack's samples may only use that pack's own concepts, so packs cannot reach into each other.
stories.seed.count: To test a list you need 200 customers, not one. Count creates that many copies of a sample record at once. You cannot use it together with an alias or repeat over.
stories.seed.data: The sample record's boxes, written like a request to the app: name 'Ana', city 'Porto'. Values can point at another sample by its alias, or ask for generated ones, such as a random name or a date. The data is realistic without typing it all.
stories.seed.id: Normally the app invents an id for each sample record. Id lets you pick one yourself, so other data or tests can point at it with certainty. It is useful for samples that others rely on.
stories.seed.repeatOver: A timetable needs one record per day and per hour: 7 days times 24 hours. Repeat over generates one record for each combination of the ranges you give. It cannot be used together with count or alias.
stories.sequence.format: Invoices should read 'INV-2026-0001', not 17. Format is the pattern of a number: the running counter padded with zeros, plus optional year, month or day. When a date part is in it, the counter starts again whenever that part changes.
stories.sequence.name: Invoice numbers and ticket numbers need counters of their own. Name labels one counter, and a box asks for its next number with that name. A pack does not rename it, so the name stays the same everywhere.
stories.sequence.scope: Two companies sharing one app each expect their invoices to start at 1. Scope decides whether one counter is shared by everyone, which is the default, or whether each tenant has its own.
